questions.q: What is the near-universal convention for importing Pandas?
options: import pandas as pd
import pandas as pandas_lib
from pandas import *
include pandas
questions.explain: You'll see 'import pandas as pd' at the top of nearly every data engineering script.

options: Pandas' table-shaped structure with rows, columns, an automatic index, and inferred per-column types
A single number stored in memory
A type of loop unique to Pandas
A file format, distinct from CSV or Parquet
questions.explain: A DataFrame is the core data structure Pandas is built around.

questions.q: How does Lesson 15's list of dictionaries relate to a DataFrame?
options: pd.DataFrame() converts a list of dictionaries directly into a real table, with each dictionary becoming one row
Lists of dictionaries cannot be converted into DataFrames
A DataFrame is a completely unrelated structure with no connection
You must first convert dictionaries into strings before creating a DataFrame
questions.explain: This is exactly the conversion this lesson demonstrates directly.

questions.q: Why does Pandas exist, instead of just using Lesson 20's manual file-reading loops?
options: Pandas replaces manual open/loop/split/convert logic with functions like pd.read_csv() that do the same job correctly in far less code
Pandas cannot read files at all, only in-memory data
Manual loops are always faster than Pandas
Pandas is only useful for writing files, never reading them
questions.explain: Lesson 22 shows pd.read_csv() doing in one line what Lesson 20 needed many lines of manual logic to approximate.
